source.title: Training, Reading, and Editing Legible Transformers

page_placements.theme: Architecture and training-time constraints (activation or weight sparsity, LWTA/TopK, decorrelation, concept supervision, gating, activation function, weight decay, non-negativity, write-disjoint experts, ViT vs ResNet) change neuron monosemanticity

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text appears intact.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures detector selectivity, vocabulary nameability, and circuit attribution in a purpose-built legible transformer. These are different measurements and a different architecture from the original neuron-pole audit.
record.gate_note: The study does not audit Qwen3-32B or score explanations generated from activating examples. Rows below cover its own measurements of unit legibility and circuit attribution; cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: Only the tool part of V4 is tested, in a new setting: a purpose-built 125M legible transformer. The paper re-reads feed-forward unit writes with a tuned lens instead of the raw logit lens. The share decodable to a nameable category rises from 38.7% to 65.3%. Final-layer units stay about 10% decodable, which the paper says is not a weak-tool effect. Most other rows measure a crisp-and-contextual 'selective' statistic. That statistic is a variance and crispness score that legibility pressures induce on purpose. The paper itself calls it detection, not naming, so it is recorded under fits_no_version. The direct-logit-attribution counts come from a small bespoke model, not attribution graphs on a large model's own neurons, so they do not bear on V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that a variance floor and a learned per-unit gate make bounded operators crisp and contextual at quality parity. Units detect far more than they name: 78% are selective, but 38.7% are raw-decodable and 65.3% with the tuned lens. Abstract concepts stay distributed with depth. Crisp units are local edit sites. Decorrelation trades reuse for editability and concentrates attribution (~15 vs ~1200 contributors in a GELU model) without raising per-unit selectivity.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a 125M-parameter transformer with bounded fuzzy set-operation feed-forward units and attention values, plus crispness, variance-floor, and learned-fraction objectives. It does not audit ordinary neurons or use the original explanation-and-scoring procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Legibility depends on objective: crispness alone collapses units; a variance floor or learned crisp fraction recovers selectivity. Readout matters: the tuned lens improves mid-layer decoding. Attention selectivity varies strongly with depth. Between-unit decorrelation changes selective fractions and circuit structure.

fits_no_version.finding: In the legible architecture, the share of crisp-and-contextual operands depends on the training objective. Crispness alone gives 2% feed-forward selective. A variance floor gives 25%, the learned fraction 78%, and decorrelation 62%. Attention selectivity rises from 18% shallow to 78% deep.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a legible-by-construction transformer, training objectives (regularization) control the share of crisp, input-dependent detector units.

fits_no_version.finding: Even with legible operators, deep abstract concepts are distributed. Late-layer blocks need rank ~256 for restoration, and single-unit ablation has median effect ~0. Token-level features, by contrast, sit on single units (AUC up to 1.00).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Abstract, non-lexical concepts in late layers are distributed across many units even when operators are legible, while token-level features are single-unit.

fits_no_version.finding: Direct logit attribution of 'than' spreads over ~1200 effective contributors in a conventional 125M GELU model, against ~15 in the decorrelated legible model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small conventional transformers, single-prediction attribution over neurons is diffuse rather than concentrated on a few units.

record.problems: All results at this scale are single seed. The model is a purpose-built legible architecture rather than an ordinary language model; several naming judgments use a category scheme, and results do not establish explanation faithfulness for ordinary neurons. The paper itself notes that selective counts are threshold-sensitive.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted detailed editing-locality measurements and most circuit-dial sweep values because they concern edit collateral or circuit shape rather than the tested claims about legibility and unit-level attribution. Omitted additional token-feature AUC rows from Table 2; R22 retains the explicitly reported newline example.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or one-job/two-job/unknown shares.
No other production models, MoE, or scale.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron re-analysis.

No InceptionV1-sized vision estimates. No interpretability-share comparison between ordinary and modern architectures: the GELU baseline has no selective or decodability numbers. Regularization effects are measured only on a selectivity statistic.
No attribution graphs on a large model's own neurons, and no comparison with a replacement model's reconstruction error.
No test of activating-example explanations predicting firing.

missing.what: Per-layer raw vs tuned decodability values, including the example layer jumping from 15% to 73% and the note that the tuned lens can hurt units already in canonical frame.
Statement that the tuned-lens recovery also applies to a GELU model, with no numbers given.

record.verdict_notes: All results are single-seed in one purpose-built 125M architecture trained to be legible. The selective statistic is threshold-fragile by the authors' own account. The only V4-relevant comparison is a readout-tool effect within this architecture. The paper offers no evidence on ordinary neurons' interpretable share.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit, pole-level job counts, or one-job/two-related-jobs/unknown categories.
The study reports one 125M-parameter, purpose-built model, not comparable shares across ordinary dense and mixture-of-experts models or at large scales.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron or recursive-generalization test.
No InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates, and no systematic comparison of architectures or tools across models. The study does test objective and readout effects on legibility in its own model.
The model is 125M parameters, not a large model; the paper uses direct logit attribution and circuit analyses, not attribution graphs, and does not evaluate reconstruction error.
No explanation written from activating examples is tested for predicting firing on separate examples.
No automated explainer-model scoring of neuron explanations on new text.

source_check.notes: Single seed, in a purpose-built bounded-unit model, not conventional neurons. 'Decodable' means logit-lens-promoted tokens fall in a seven-way category dictionary. 65.3% is either-frame (raw or own tuned); tuned-only is not reported. 38.7% and 65.3% are whole-model figures, although l0's condition says mid-stack.

statements.correction: Annealed model, all layers: 38.7% (7131 of 18432) of FFN operands decode through the raw logit lens to a nameable content category (seven-way dictionary). 65.3% decode in either the raw or the unit's own tuned frame. The gain concentrates mid-stack (one layer 15% to 73%). Single seed.
statements.problem: 65.3% is the share decodable in either the raw or the unit's own tuned frame, not through the tuned lens alone. The text notes the lens can hurt units that were already canonical, so tuned-only would be lower. Also, 38.7% and 65.3% are whole-model figures (all 18432 operands), not mid-stack. 'Decode' means to a nameable content category, not to a single token.

statements.correction: 2607.08946 (125M bounded-unit LM, single seed): decorrelation λd 0→1 in otherwise unchanged training. Selective% goes 78.7→62.2, non-monotone. A concept's co-firing group goes from a median 562 units to a single unit. A variance floor on top of the crispness penalty raises FFN selective from 2% to 25%. These are purpose-built legibility objectives on bounded operands. The study does not test conventional regularization (weight decay, dropout) as a cause of messy neurons in standard LMs.
statements.problem: The quoted basis line is the catalog record's untested line, not a claim about the paper's wording, so that is fine. But for this study, 'LM studies do not isolate regularization' is too broad. It sweeps a between-unit decorrelation regularizer in otherwise unchanged LM training. It also varies crispness and variance-floor penalties, and reports their effects on unit selectivity and concept localization.

statements.correction: Raw logit lens 38.7% vs either-frame (raw or own tuned) 65.3%, whole model. The gain is mid-stack. Final layer ~10%, with the lens near identity there; authors call it genuine, not rotation.
statements.problem: 'Raw logit lens vs tuned lens: 38.7% vs 65.3%' mislabels the 65.3%, which is the share decodable in either the raw or the unit's own tuned frame. 'Final layer ~10% either way' is a fair inference from the near-identity lens, but the text gives no separate raw and tuned final-layer numbers.
